item.title: Momentic Mo
item.description:
Mo takes an exploratory approach to testing. Instead of writing scripts for each test, a team points Mo at an app and supplies login credentials, and AI agents navigate the interface, trying flows, entering unusual inputs, and checking for errors or broken behavior. The agents report what they find.

Momentic’s wider platform helps teams write and maintain end-to-end tests in natural language, which reduces upkeep when interfaces change. Mo complements that by finding issues no one thought to test, like a human tester poking around.

item.title: NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform
item.description:
The platform responds to a security worry: autonomous agents that can run commands and access data need limits that a compromised agent cannot disable. OpenShell is an open-source runtime that places each agent in its own sandbox with policy-based permissions, and a prover checks that granted permissions cannot combine into something the operator did not intend.

Sentry adds enforcement outside the agent’s machine. It runs on BlueField data processing units, which sit apart from the host, so it can watch behavior and isolate an agent quickly even if the host is compromised. NVIDIA has described it as a reference design, with many partners integrating the pieces.

item.title: QA Wolf
item.description:
QA Wolf offers testing as a service. Instead of a company writing and maintaining its own automated tests, QA Wolf’s team creates Playwright tests for the critical flows, runs them in parallel on every release, and fixes tests when the app changes. They report real bugs, and filter flaky failures.

AI generates and repairs tests, while engineers verify results. The aim is high coverage without the burden of test maintenance, which often overwhelms small teams. Tests are written in open frameworks, so customers own the code.

item.title: Ivo
item.description:
Ivo is an AI contract review tool built for in-house legal teams. A lawyer opens an incoming contract, and Ivo compares it with the team’s preferred positions, flags issues, and suggests redlines in the document, using the editor the lawyer already works in.

Beyond review, Ivo has added tools to manage the whole flow. Business users submit requests, contracts are routed to the right reviewers, negotiations are tracked, and approvals are collected. A repository holds executed agreements for analysis.

item.title: Natural
item.description:
Natural addresses a gap in agent infrastructure: how an AI agent pays for things. Through its API, developers create an account for an agent, fund it, set spending rules, and let it pay vendors, receive money, or issue virtual cards for purchases.

Controls matter, since a spending agent can cause damage. Limits, approvals, and logs let the owner decide what an agent may buy and see what it did. The company positions this as payments infrastructure for a future where agents transact with each other and with businesses.

item.title: OpenAI Daybreak
item.description:
Daybreak gives defenders access to frontier AI for security work. Approved organizations use models for tasks such as triaging incidents, analyzing malware, validating patches, and hunting for vulnerabilities, with workflows designed for security teams.

OpenAI split access into tiers. A defender tier provides frontier models without some of the safeguards that might block legitimate security prompts, and a more specialized tier provides models trained for higher-risk testing such as vulnerability research and exploit validation. Access is limited to vetted individuals and organizations.

item.title: AI for Developers
item.description:
AI for Developers is written for people who build software and want to use AI well. Issues tend to focus on how to do things: setting up an AI coding assistant, writing prompts for common programming tasks, comparing tools, or building small projects with language model APIs. The tone is practical rather than speculative.

A developer-focused newsletter fills a gap between general AI news and academic papers. Readers look for ideas they can apply the same day, such as workflows for code review, testing, or documentation, and for honest comparisons that show what works and what does not. The Substack format also lets readers comment and share tips.

item.title: Altern Newsletter
item.description:
The Altern Newsletter comes from Altern, a site that catalogs AI tools. Each issue gathers newly launched products and resources the team found that week, with a short description of what each does. It is organized so a reader can skim for tools relevant to their work.

A weekly cadence keeps it manageable for busy readers. The content leans toward product discovery, not deep analysis, so it works well alongside news-focused newsletters. Items come from the team’s directory and community submissions, which means selection reflects what makers share.

item.title: Superhuman AI
item.description:
Superhuman AI is a free daily email aimed at professionals who want to apply AI at work. Issues summarize news in brief, then spend time on practical advice: tools worth trying, prompts that work, and ways to save time.

The audience skews toward business users and non-technical readers rather than researchers. The newsletter is supported by sponsors, which are labeled, and has grown to one of the larger AI newsletters.

item.title: The Neuron
item.description:
The Neuron is a free email for people who want to follow AI without a technical background. Each issue picks a few stories, explains them in accessible language, and points to tools worth trying. The tone is conversational and avoids excessive jargon.

It includes practical sections, such as prompts and tutorials, and links to its own resources. The newsletter is supported by sponsors, which are labeled.

It is free. As with other daily newsletters, coverage is selective. Alternatives include The Rundown AI, Superhuman AI, TLDR AI, Ben’s Bites, and The Batch. The Neuron suits professionals who want a quick daily AI update.

item.title: The Rundown AI
item.description:
The Rundown AI is one of the most widely read AI newsletters. Each issue covers major stories, new tools, and research in a few minutes of reading, with a consistent format that makes it easy to skim. Sections highlight top stories, quick hits, and tools.

Beyond the newsletter, the brand offers a community, courses, and a product directory. Sponsorship supports the free edition.

The Rundown AI is free. Daily newsletters can repeat the same headlines, so readers often choose one or two. Alternatives include The Neuron, TLDR AI, Superhuman AI, Ben’s Bites, and The Batch. The Rundown AI suits people who want a fast daily briefing.

item.title: ManyChat
item.description: ManyChat lets businesses and creators respond to people in direct messages at scale. A visual flow builder defines how a conversation proceeds: someone comments a keyword on an Instagram post, ManyChat sends a DM with a link or a guide, asks questions, collects an email address, and tags the contact. It is widely used by influencers and online businesses to deliver lead magnets, run giveaways, and sell products through chat.

item.title: Neon
item.description:
Neon rebuilt Postgres for the cloud by separating storage from compute. That design lets a database scale up under load and scale down to zero when idle, so you pay for use instead of keeping a server running. Developers get standard Postgres, which means existing tools, drivers, and extensions work, including pgvector for storing embeddings in AI applications.

The standout feature is branching. Because storage is copy-on-write, you can create a full copy of a database in seconds, like a Git branch, for testing a migration, running a preview environment for each pull request, or giving each developer an isolated copy. The same ability makes Neon attractive to AI coding agents and platforms that spin up many short-lived databases. Connection pooling, read replicas, and integrations with Vercel and other platforms are available.

item.title: Transifex
item.description:
Transifex helps product teams translate content into many languages. Developers connect repositories such as GitHub and GitLab, or use a command-line tool, and new text is sent to Transifex for translation. Translators and reviewers work in an online editor with translation memory, glossaries, and context, and approved translations flow back to the codebase.

A distinctive piece is Transifex Native, which lets apps fetch translations through an SDK, so updating a translation doesn’t require a new release. AI and machine translation pre-translate content, and quality checks flag issues, while workflows route text through reviewers or professional translation vendors. Integrations cover design tools, content management systems, and help centers.

item.title: DroneDeploy
item.description:
DroneDeploy is a platform for drone data. Users plan an automated flight from a tablet or phone, the drone captures images, and the software stitches them into orthomosaic maps and 3D models. From these, it can measure distances, areas, and volumes, such as a stockpile or excavation.

Repeat flights show progress. Construction teams compare site conditions to plans, farmers monitor crop health, and mining operations measure material movement. AI detects objects and changes, and the platform has expanded to capture from ground robots and 360 cameras for indoor progress tracking.

item.title: Exscientia
item.description:
Exscientia designed small-molecule drug candidates with AI models and ran automated labs to synthesize and test the top predictions. Results fed back into the models to improve the next round, a closed loop that aimed to shorten discovery time and reduce the number of compounds that must be made.

The company worked on cancer and other diseases, and formed partnerships with large pharmaceutical firms. It was among the first to move AI-designed molecules into clinical trials. After a period of strategic changes, it combined with Recursion, which brought together Recursion’s biology data and Exscientia’s chemistry design and automated synthesis.

item.title: Isomorphic Labs
item.description:
Isomorphic Labs aims to use AI to design medicines. It builds on DeepMind’s work on predicting protein structures and extends the idea to the interactions between proteins and drug molecules, so models can propose compounds that bind to a target. The goal is to reduce the time and cost of finding candidates.

Rather than selling software, the company runs drug discovery programs, both on its own and in collaboration with pharmaceutical companies. It has described building a platform that can be applied across diseases, with early efforts in areas such as oncology and immunology.

item.title: Overjet
item.description:
Overjet is dental AI that reads radiographs. When a dentist takes X-rays, the software outlines suspected cavities, measures bone levels, and identifies calculus and other issues, giving a second look that supports diagnosis and helps explain problems to patients by showing them the marked images.

The technology also serves payers. Insurers use it to review claims and check whether treatment matches findings, and large dental groups use it to standardize care across offices. It has regulatory clearance for several functions in the US.

item.title: PagerDuty
item.description:
PagerDuty is an incident management platform. Monitoring tools send alerts, and PagerDuty decides who should respond based on schedules and escalation rules, notifying them by phone, text, or app. It groups related alerts so one problem does not create a flood of pages.

During an incident, it supports coordination: a timeline, chat integrations, status pages, and runbooks for common fixes. AI features summarize the situation, suggest causes based on past incidents, and help write postmortems. Automation can run diagnostic or remediation steps.

item.title: Pearl
item.description:
Pearl focuses on dental radiograph analysis. Dentists upload X-rays, and the Second Opinion tool highlights suspected problems, such as caries, calculus, and periapical lesions, in real time, which helps catch issues and show patients the findings.

The company has expanded into other uses, including claims review for insurers and tools for dental service organizations that want consistent standards across offices. It holds regulatory clearances for several of its functions.

Pearl is sold on subscription to practices and organizations. AI findings need dentist confirmation, and insurers using AI on claims draw scrutiny. Alternatives include Overjet, VideaHealth, Denti.AI, Dentrix Detect, and Align’s tools. Pearl suits dental practices adding AI radiograph review.

item.title: Pix4D
item.description:
Pix4D is photogrammetry software. Photos taken by a drone or a camera are processed into orthomosaics, digital surface models, and 3D meshes with accurate coordinates, so users can measure distances, areas, and volumes from the results.

Products target different jobs. One handles mapping from drones, another focuses on surveying with scanners and phones, and others serve fields like agriculture and inspection. AI helps classify features and clean up point clouds, and cloud processing handles big projects.

item.title: Skydio
item.description:
Skydio drones fly themselves safely. Cameras and onboard computing let the drone see its surroundings and avoid obstacles in real time, even in complex places such as under bridges or around structures, which reduces crashes and operator skill demands.

Software supports missions: automated inspection routes, 3D scans of structures, and live video for first responders. Docks let drones launch and land on their own for repeated tasks. Customers include police and fire departments, utilities, infrastructure inspectors, and defense agencies.

item.title: Cellebrite
item.description:
Cellebrite is a digital forensics company. Its tools pull data from mobile devices, cloud accounts, and computers, including deleted items where possible, and organize it so investigators can review messages, photos, locations, and app activity. The company serves police, intelligence agencies, and corporate security teams.

Analysis products help investigators manage large amounts of data. AI can classify images, search through text, find connections between people and devices, and build timelines. Cloud platforms support collaboration across a case and sharing evidence with prosecutors.

item.title: Crisalix
item.description:
Crisalix builds simulation tools for aesthetic medicine. A surgeon takes photos of a patient, the software builds a 3D model of the face or body, and the surgeon adjusts parameters to show what a procedure might look like. Patients can see and discuss options before deciding.

The aim is to improve communication and set realistic expectations. A visual helps patients and surgeons align on goals, and consultations can be more productive. The company sells to plastic surgeons, dermatologists, and clinics, and has tools for marketing and patient engagement.

item.title: ESHA Genesis R&D
item.description:
Genesis R&D is a long-standing tool for food product development. A formulator enters ingredients and amounts, and the software calculates nutrients using a large food database, then generates a nutrition facts panel and an ingredient list formatted for regulatory requirements in different countries.

It also helps with design choices. Users can compare formulas, adjust ingredients to hit targets for calories, sodium, or protein, check claims such as low fat or high fiber, and flag allergens. These features reduce the risk of labeling errors, which can lead to recalls.

item.title: Givebutter
item.description:
Givebutter is a fundraising platform for nonprofits. Organizations create donation forms, run crowdfunding and peer-to-peer campaigns, sell event tickets, and accept recurring gifts. Its donor CRM keeps a record of each supporter’s giving and communications.

The platform tries to be affordable for small groups. It has been known for a model where donors can choose to tip the platform rather than the nonprofit paying fees. Auctions, text-to-give, and email tools are included. AI helps segment lists and draft appeals and thank-yous.

item.title: Holistiplan
item.description:
Holistiplan helps financial advisors use tax returns in planning. An advisor uploads a client’s return, and the software extracts the figures and generates a summary showing income, deductions, brackets, and observations. It highlights ideas worth discussing, such as Roth conversions, capital gains harvesting, or the timing of donations.

Scenarios let advisors model the effect of a strategy on taxes. Reports are designed to be shared with clients, helping advisors show value beyond investments. AI assists with reading documents and drafting talking points.

item.title: Trainerize
item.description:
Trainerize is a coaching platform for fitness professionals. Trainers create programs from an exercise library, assign them to clients, and monitor workouts logged in a mobile app. Messaging, habit tracking, and progress photos keep clients engaged.

Additional features include nutrition coaching, integrations with wearables, payment processing, and a branded app. AI helps draft programs and suggest changes based on adherence and goals.

Trainerize has a free tier for a small number of clients and paid plans. It is owned by ABC Fitness. Alternatives include TrueCoach, Everfit, PT Distinction, Mindbody, and Hevy Coach. Trainerize suits independent trainers and gyms.

item.title: Unit21
item.description:
Unit21 is a risk and compliance platform. It ingests transaction and customer data, flags suspicious activity with rules and machine learning, and routes alerts to analysts through case management. Teams build and adjust rules in a no-code interface.

The platform covers fraud prevention, anti-money laundering monitoring, and onboarding checks, and generates reports such as suspicious activity filings. AI agents help summarize cases and speed investigations.

Unit21 is sold to fintechs, banks, and marketplaces on custom pricing. Alerts need tuning to avoid overload. Alternatives include Sardine, Feedzai, Alloy, ComplyAdvantage, and Actimize. Unit21 suits risk teams at financial companies.

item.title: EnergyCAP
item.description:
EnergyCAP collects utility bills and meter data and puts them into one system. Facility managers, energy consultants, and sustainability teams use it to track electricity, gas, water, and other utilities across a portfolio, pay bills, and report on costs and emissions.

Analytics find savings. The software flags bills with errors, such as duplicate charges or wrong rates, and highlights usage that departs from normal patterns, which may point to equipment problems. Benchmarking compares buildings, and reports support sustainability disclosures and incentive programs.

item.title: 8th Wall
item.description:
8th Wall made AR available through a link. Developers built experiences using web technologies, and users opened them in a phone browser by scanning a QR code or tapping a link, with no app download. Brands used it for marketing campaigns, product try-ons, games, and events, and agencies liked that it worked across iOS and Android. Features included world tracking, image targets, face effects, and, later, location-based AR.

Niantic, the company behind Pokémon Go, acquired 8th Wall, and its technology was used alongside Niantic’s mapping and spatial work. Niantic Spatial, the spinoff focused on geospatial AI, then ended access to the 8th Wall platform. Hosted projects were given time to keep running, and the engine was released as open source, so developers can still use its code.

item.title: accessiBe
item.description:
accessiBe promises to make websites more accessible with minimal effort. A line of code adds an accessibility interface for visitors, with options such as larger text, contrast adjustments, and keyboard navigation, while AI runs in the background to detect issues like missing image descriptions and improper labels and attempt to fix them. Businesses use it to reduce the risk of accessibility lawsuits and to serve users with disabilities.

The company has built other products, including audits, monitoring, and expert-assisted remediation. It reports compliance status and offers statements that businesses can publish. Its marketing emphasized automation and quick compliance.

item.title: Adobe Character Animator
item.description:
Character Animator brings puppets to life. You prepare a character in Photoshop or Illustrator with layers for eyes, mouth, and body parts, import it, and the software maps your face and voice to the character. As you speak and move, the character blinks, talks, and reacts in real time, with lip sync generated from your audio.

It was designed for speed. Rigged characters can be recorded live, and the performance can be edited afterward on a timeline. Triggers set up with keyboard keys can switch poses, props, or expressions. The tool has been used for animated shows, live broadcasts, and explainer videos, and it integrates with Premiere Pro and After Effects.

item.title: Agiloft
item.description:
Agiloft is a configurable system for managing contracts from request to renewal. Teams create agreements from templates and clause libraries, route them through approvals, negotiate with redlining, collect signatures, and store them in a searchable repository. Alerts remind owners of renewals and obligations, and reports show how contracts are performing, so legal, procurement, and sales teams share a single source of truth.

Its design emphasizes flexibility without custom coding. Organizations can adjust fields, workflows, and rules through no-code tools, which suits companies with unusual processes, and it connects with systems such as Salesforce, SAP, and DocuSign. AI features extract data from existing contracts, identify risky or missing clauses, summarize agreements, and let users ask questions in plain language, which speeds up migration from messy archives.

item.title: Alchemy
item.description:
Alchemy gives developers a reliable way to talk to blockchains. Running your own Ethereum node takes expertise and hardware, so most teams rent access instead. Alchemy offers that through APIs that read data, send transactions, and subscribe to events, supporting Ethereum and many other networks, including layer 2 chains. Its infrastructure is built for uptime and speed, which matters when an app depends on real-time chain data.

On top of raw node access are higher-level tools. Enhanced APIs return token balances, NFT metadata, transaction history, and transfers in a form that is easier to use than raw blockchain data. Smart wallet and account abstraction tools let apps create wallets and sponsor gas fees for users, rollup services help teams launch their own chains, and webhooks and subgraphs deliver data to applications. Dashboards show request volume, errors, and latency.

item.title: Amwell
item.description:
Amwell provides the technology behind a lot of virtual care. Hospitals and health systems use it to run telehealth programs for their own patients, health plans offer it as a benefit, and employers use it to give workers access to remote visits. Patients can see a clinician by video for urgent care, primary care, behavioral health, and specialty care, with scheduling, intake, and visit tools in one platform.

It also offers services around the visit. These include a hospital-grade platform for remote consultations within hospitals, digital programs for chronic conditions, and a network of clinicians for companies that don’t have their own. AI features help with intake, triage, and documentation, and the platform integrates with electronic health records. Its ability to be customized for each client is a selling point.

item.title: Applitools
item.description: Applitools solves a problem that ordinary automated tests miss: whether a page looks correct. A functional test can confirm a button exists while the layout is broken, overlapping, or off-screen. Applitools Eyes takes screenshots during tests and compares them to approved baselines using a visual AI that understands layout, text, and color the way a person would. That avoids the flood of false alarms from pixel-by-pixel comparison, where tiny rendering differences trip every check.

item.title: Arcadia
item.description:
Arcadia has two sides. For consumers, it helps people use renewable energy even if they cannot install solar panels. Customers subscribe to a share of a local community solar project and receive credits on their utility bill, or choose plans that match their usage with renewable generation. The platform tracks bills and savings in one account.

For businesses, Arcadia offers access to utility data. It connects to thousands of utilities to pull bill and usage information through APIs, which energy software companies, solar developers, and sustainability teams use to analyze consumption. This data layer is a major part of its business and helps other companies build energy products.

item.title: ArcGIS
item.description: ArcGIS is the leading commercial GIS platform. Governments, utilities, environmental agencies, city planners, and businesses use it to collect location data, display it on maps, and analyze spatial relationships, such as which neighborhoods lie within a flood zone or where to place a new store. The product family includes ArcGIS Pro for desktop analysis, ArcGIS Online as a cloud service for building and sharing maps, and ArcGIS Enterprise for organizations that run their own servers.

item.title: Archbee
item.description:
Archbee helps teams write and publish documentation. The editor supports rich text, code blocks, diagrams, and embedded content, and spaces organize material into sections with navigation and search. Teams can keep docs private for internal use or publish them as polished public sites with custom domains and branding, which makes it suitable for product help centers and developer portals.

Features for technical documentation include API reference generation from OpenAPI specs, Git integration to sync docs with repositories, version control, and review workflows. AI features provide smarter search and an assistant that answers questions from your documentation, plus writing help. Analytics show which pages are read and what readers search for but cannot find.

item.title: Arterys
item.description:
Arterys was an early company in medical imaging AI. Its cloud platform ran deep-learning tools on scans such as cardiac MRI, chest CT, and liver studies, helping radiologists and cardiologists measure and analyze images faster. It was among the first companies to receive regulatory clearance in the United States for a deep-learning clinical application, and its viewer was designed to be used inside the browser without special workstations.

The platform’s main idea was to embed AI directly in the workflow clinicians already use. It connected to hospital systems such as PACS and electronic health records, so results appeared alongside the images instead of in a separate tool. Automating routine measurements, like heart chamber volumes, could save time and reduce variation between readers.

item.title: Atomwise
item.description:
Atomwise applies machine learning to the early stage of drug discovery. Its AtomNet technology uses deep learning to predict how well a small molecule would bind to a protein, which lets researchers screen enormous virtual libraries of compounds before running physical experiments. The idea is to cut down the number of molecules a lab has to test, so teams find promising candidates faster and spend less on dead ends.

The company works through partnerships with pharmaceutical firms, biotech startups, and academic labs, covering many disease targets, including some that have been hard to address with conventional methods. Beyond screening, it has developed methods to search ultra-large chemical spaces and tools for designing and optimizing compounds. It also runs internal programs, so it is both a technology provider and a drug developer.

item.title: Audible
item.description:
Audible made audiobooks mainstream. Members get monthly credits to buy audiobooks they keep, plus access to a catalog of included titles, podcasts, and originals, and they can listen through the app on phones, tablets, and smart speakers. Features such as variable speed, bookmarks, sleep timers, and syncing between listening and reading with Kindle books make it practical for commuting and chores.

Technology is changing how titles are made. Audible has been introducing AI narration for publishers and authors who cannot afford a human narrator, and AI-powered translation and dubbing for audiobooks, alongside AI-based recommendations and summaries. Human narrators remain central to the premium experience, and the shift has prompted debate among narrators and listeners about quality and the future of the profession.

item.title: Augury
item.description:
Augury helps factories and facilities avoid unexpected equipment failures. Small wireless sensors attach to machines such as motors, pumps, fans, and compressors and measure vibration, temperature, and other signals. The data goes to the cloud, where machine learning models trained on large numbers of machines identify patterns that signal a developing problem, such as bearing wear or misalignment, often weeks before a breakdown.

The platform sends alerts with a diagnosis and recommended action, so maintenance teams can plan repairs during scheduled downtime instead of reacting to a failure. Dashboards show the health of assets across plants, and the service has expanded to include process monitoring and insights into production performance. Industries include food and beverage, chemicals, pulp and paper, and building management.

item.title: Aurora Solar
item.description:
Aurora Solar is used by solar installers, designers, and sales teams. A designer enters an address and the software builds a 3D model of the property from aerial imagery and lidar data, including trees and nearby buildings that cast shade. It then lays out panels, models how much electricity the system will produce across the year, and calculates savings and payback so a homeowner sees the economics.

Aurora automates much of the work that used to take hours. AI generates roof models and code-compliant panel layouts in minutes, handles stringing and fire pathways, and prepares permit-ready plan sets. Sales tools produce branded proposals and handle financing options and contracts, and drone mapping can capture detail for larger or more complex sites. For commercial projects, the platform covers larger arrays and different incentives.

item.title: Autodesk Construction Cloud
item.description:
Autodesk Construction Cloud brings together the tools that general contractors, owners, and subcontractors use to run building projects. A shared data environment keeps drawings, models, and documents in one place with version control, so everyone works from the current set. Teams use it for design review, model coordination across disciplines, quantity takeoff, cost estimating, issue tracking, and quality and safety checks in the field.

Autodesk has been folding the product line into Forma, its industry cloud, and the construction products now carry the Forma name, such as Forma Build, Forma Data Management, Forma Takeoff, and Forma Estimate. They connect to Autodesk’s design tools like Revit, which keeps information flowing from the design model to the construction site. AI features help automate routine work and surface insights, for example by flagging risks, extracting information from documents, or speeding up takeoff.

item.title: AutoGrid
item.description:
AutoGrid builds software for the changing electricity grid. As more homes and businesses add solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles, utilities need ways to coordinate them. AutoGrid’s platform forecasts supply and demand, controls devices, and combines many small resources into virtual power plants that can respond when the grid needs help. Machine learning predicts energy use and optimizes when to charge, discharge, or reduce load.

Utilities and energy retailers use it to run demand response programs, manage commercial and residential batteries, and monetize flexibility in energy markets. It integrates with device makers and energy management systems, so a single platform can orchestrate thermostats, batteries, EV chargers, and industrial loads. The goal is to lower costs and reduce the need for new power plants during peak demand.

item.title: Avalara
item.description: Avalara helps businesses get indirect taxes right. Sales tax rules vary by state, city, product type, and customer, and rates change often, which makes manual calculation risky. Avalara integrates with online stores, accounting software, and ERP systems to calculate the correct tax at checkout or invoicing based on the transaction’s location and product, then helps file returns and remit payments in many jurisdictions. It covers sales and use tax, VAT, and other transaction taxes around the world.

item.title: AWS IoT Core
item.description:
AWS IoT Core is the entry point for Internet of Things devices into AWS. Devices connect using MQTT, HTTPS, and other protocols, authenticate with certificates, and publish and receive messages, with the service scaling to billions of devices and trillions of messages. A device registry tracks each device, and Device Shadows keep a copy of the device’s state so applications can interact with it even when it is offline.

A rules engine processes incoming data and routes it to other AWS services such as Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, Kinesis, and SageMaker, so data can be stored, analyzed, or used to trigger actions. Related services handle device management, fleet monitoring, over-the-air updates, and edge computing with AWS IoT Greengrass, which runs code and machine learning models on the device. Security features include fine-grained policies, and logging and monitoring tools.

item.title: Azure Content Moderator
item.description:
Content Moderator was Microsoft’s tool for checking user-generated content. It scanned text for profanity and personal data, analyzed images for adult or racy content, and screened video, returning scores and flags that platforms could use to filter or send items for human review. Online communities, marketplaces, and apps with user uploads used it as an automated first line of defense.

Microsoft has deprecated the service and no longer allows new projects, directing customers to Azure AI Content Safety. The newer service uses more advanced models, handles multiple severity levels across categories such as hate, sexual content, violence, and self-harm, supports many more languages, and adds features aimed at generative AI, including prompt shields and groundedness detection. Existing Content Moderator projects continue to work until the retirement date.

item.title: Azure IoT Hub
item.description: Azure IoT Hub is the messaging backbone for connected devices on Azure. Devices send telemetry such as sensor readings to the cloud, and the cloud can send commands and configuration back. Each device has its own identity and credentials, so the platform can authenticate it, and connections use standard protocols like MQTT and AMQP. The hub scales to large fleets and can route messages to storage, stream processing, and analytics services.

item.title: Bambu Studio
item.description:
Bambu Studio turns 3D model files into instructions a printer can follow. You load a model, arrange it on the virtual build plate, set options such as layer height, supports, and infill, and the slicer generates the toolpath, previewing how the print will be built. It supports multicolor and multimaterial printing through Bambu’s automatic material system, with tools to assign colors and manage waste.

It is based on open-source slicer code and is itself open source. Features include automatic calibration, print profiles tuned for Bambu printers and common filaments, remote monitoring and control over the cloud, and integration with MakerWorld, Bambu’s online library of models, where users share designs and print profiles. It runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux and also supports some other printers.

item.title: Be My Eyes
item.description: Be My Eyes connects people who cannot see well with help. In the app, a blind or low-vision user can start a video call, and a sighted volunteer sees through the camera and helps with a task such as reading an expiry date, matching colors, finding a dropped item, or navigating an unfamiliar place. Millions of volunteers around the world have signed up, which means that help is usually available quickly, at any hour.

item.title: Benchling
item.description: Benchling brings the scattered tasks of a research lab into one cloud system. Scientists use the notebook to record experiments, design DNA and protein sequences with molecular biology tools, and register the samples and materials they create, so everything is traceable. Teams track workflows, share results, and connect lab instruments, which replaces a mix of spreadsheets, paper notebooks, and separate databases. It is common at startups and large biopharma companies.

item.title: BetterHelp
item.description:
BetterHelp is one of the largest online therapy platforms. You fill out a questionnaire about your needs and preferences, and the service suggests a licensed counselor. You can message your therapist, join live sessions by video, phone, or chat, and schedule at times that suit you, which removes commuting and makes weekly care easier for many people. Therapists are independent licensed professionals such as psychologists, social workers, and counselors.

The pricing model is a recurring subscription based on location and therapist, rather than per-visit billing, and it generally does not accept insurance, which some people find convenient and others find expensive. It is owned by Teladoc Health. Some reviewers praise the convenience and access, while others report difficulty finding a good match or a pushy sales process. Therapy that happens in messages works differently from a weekly hour in an office, and some people prefer live sessions.

item.title: BetterUp
item.description:
BetterUp sells coaching to organizations as a benefit for employees. Each person is matched with a coach based on goals such as becoming a better manager, handling stress, improving communication, or preparing for a promotion. Sessions take place by video, with coaches who are credentialed and trained in a consistent method. The company also includes assessments, programs for managers, and group sessions, and it publishes research on its results.

Technology plays a growing role. AI tools supplement human coaches by offering reflection prompts, summarizing sessions, suggesting next steps, and giving employees an always-available assistant for quick questions. Dashboards give employers aggregate data on participation and outcomes, without exposing individual conversations. Programs can be scaled for small teams or an entire company.

item.title: BigID
item.description:
BigID starts with a question many companies cannot answer: where is our sensitive data? It scans databases, file shares, cloud storage, SaaS apps, and data lakes to discover personal information, financial records, and other regulated data, then classifies it using machine learning. The results build a catalog showing what data exists, where it sits, and who can access it. That map is the basis for privacy and security work.

Several functions build on the catalog. Privacy teams use it to respond to access and deletion requests, track consent, and meet rules like GDPR and CCPA. Security teams use it to find overexposed data, fix permissions, and reduce risk through remediation workflows. A newer focus is AI governance: the platform identifies which AI agents, copilots, and models can reach sensitive data, helps limit that access, and checks against frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act.

item.title: Bizzabo
item.description: Bizzabo is a software platform for corporate and large-scale event teams. Planners build event websites, sell tickets and handle registration, manage speakers and agendas, and track who attends. On site, it supports badge printing and check-in, and a mobile app lets attendees see the schedule, message each other, and use polls or Q&A during sessions. For virtual and hybrid events, it can stream sessions and bring remote attendees into the same experience.

item.title: Blinkist
item.description:
Blinkist is designed for people who want the main ideas of a book without reading all of it. Editors and writers distill nonfiction titles in business, psychology, science, health, and self-improvement into short summaries, with key takeaways and often a quick audio version. Users listen on a commute or skim on a break, and it’s used as a way to preview a book before deciding to read it fully.

The app has broadened with audiobooks, original content, and tools such as highlighting and collections of titles by topic. AI features include personalized recommendations and generated summaries or answers based on its library, and an AI assistant that lets users ask questions about topics. Audio can be downloaded for offline listening.

item.title: Bloomerang
item.description: Bloomerang is built around donor retention, which is one of the hardest problems in fundraising: many donors give once and never again. The CRM stores each supporter’s contact details, gifts, communications, and notes, and it shows a timeline of every interaction. A generosity score and engagement level help staff see who is likely to give again and who may be slipping away, so they can focus outreach where it counts.

item.title: Bonterra
item.description:
Bonterra was created by combining several nonprofit software companies, including EveryAction, Social Solutions, Network for Good, and CyberGrants. That heritage explains the breadth: the company sells tools for fundraising and donor management, case management for human services programs, volunteer and employee giving programs, grants administration, and online giving pages. Nonprofits can use pieces of it or adopt a larger suite.

The pitch is to connect the work of raising money with the work of delivering programs. A charity can track a donor’s giving next to the services it funds, and a case manager can record outcomes that feed into reports for funders. AI features appear in tasks like drafting fundraising messages, segmenting supporters, and summarizing case notes, with attention to privacy because the data can be sensitive.

item.title: Bugsnag
item.description: Bugsnag tells engineering teams what is breaking in their software and for whom. A small SDK in a web, mobile, or server app reports crashes and handled errors with a stack trace, device and browser details, user information, and the actions that led up to the failure. Instead of a flood of raw events, Bugsnag groups similar errors together, so a single bug appears as one issue with a count of affected users.

item.title: Buildxact
item.description:
Buildxact is built for builders who work from plans and spreadsheets and need a more organized way to price jobs. Users can create estimates from templates and cost catalogs, perform takeoffs from digital plans, and turn the estimate into a professional proposal. After a job is won, the same data feeds purchase orders, schedules, and cost tracking, so you can compare what you estimated with what you spent.

The software covers the flow of a residential project: estimating, quoting, selections, job scheduling, subcontractor coordination, and invoicing, with integrations to accounting software such as QuickBooks and Xero. AI features help read plans and speed up takeoffs, suggest items, and draft proposals. It targets small to mid-sized companies, such as custom home builders, remodelers, and specialty trades.

item.title: Calm
item.description:
Calm is one of the most downloaded wellness apps. Its content library includes guided meditations of different lengths, sleep stories read by narrators in a soothing voice, calming music, breathing exercises, and masterclasses on topics such as stress and focus. A daily session and reminders encourage a habit. Many people use it mainly to fall asleep, which is where the app is strongest.

The company has extended into other areas. Calm Health offers programs for employers and health plans, with tools for sleep, stress, and mental wellbeing, and content for kids and families. Personalization suggests content based on your goals and mood, and newer features use AI to tailor recommendations. The app is not a substitute for therapy, but it can support relaxation and routines.

item.title: Catapult Sports
item.description: Catapult makes the small wearable devices that professional teams use to measure what athletes do. A tracker worn in a vest sits against the athlete’s upper back and records movement with GPS and inertial sensors, capturing distance, speed, accelerations, impacts, and the intensity of effort. Coaches and sports scientists use the data to see how hard each player is working, compare training with match demands, and adjust loads to reduce the risk of injury.

item.title: Character Creator
item.description: Character Creator lets artists build 3D characters without modeling every detail. You start with a base body, adjust shape sliders for face and body, and apply skin, hair, clothing, and accessories from a library. A rigged skeleton and facial controls come ready to animate, so a character can be used right away in games, films, and animations. Pipelines to Unreal Engine, Unity, Blender, Maya, and other tools make it practical in production.

item.title: CloudHealth by VMware
item.description: CloudHealth was one of the first tools built for managing cloud costs across several providers. Companies connect their AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts and get a consolidated view of spending, broken down by team, project, or application using tags and rules. Reports show where money goes, budgets raise alerts when spending drifts, and recommendations point to unused resources and oversized instances. That helps finance and engineering teams share a view of cloud costs.

item.title: Coggle
item.description:
Coggle keeps mind mapping simple. In the browser, you start with a central idea and add branches by clicking, using colors, images, and text, and the diagram grows into a tidy tree. It can also draw flowcharts, with free-form connections between nodes, so the same tool covers brainstorming, note taking, planning, and basic process diagrams. The look is clean, with auto-arranged branches that make diagrams easy to read.

Collaboration is a core feature. Several people can edit the same diagram at once and see each other’s changes, and a full history lets you review and restore earlier versions. Diagrams can include notes and images, be shared by link, and be exported as PDF, image, or text outlines. Students, teachers, and small teams use it for study notes, lesson plans, and project outlines.

item.title: Confluence AI
item.description:
Confluence is where many teams keep their documentation. It organizes pages into spaces, with templates for meeting notes, product requirements, runbooks, project plans, and knowledge bases. Pages support rich formatting, comments, and embedded content from Jira and other tools. Version history and permissions help control who can edit and read what. Teams in engineering, product, IT, and operations use it as a shared source of truth.

AI features come through Atlassian’s Rovo. Inside Confluence, you can summarize a long page, draft content from a short prompt, improve or translate writing, and ask questions in natural language and get answers drawn from the knowledge in your spaces. Rovo search reaches across Confluence, Jira, and connected tools like Google Drive and Slack, and agents can take on tasks such as turning a meeting note into action items.

item.title: Covariant
item.description: Covariant started in robotics research with a goal of building a general model that could control robots in the physical world. Its first big application was robotic picking, in which a robot arm takes products from bins and places them into orders. That task is hard because warehouses contain thousands of different items with varied shapes, materials, and packaging. Covariant Brain, its AI system, was trained on data from many deployments to deal with that variety, instead of being programmed for each product.

item.title: Creately
item.description:
Creately combines diagramming and whiteboarding in one workspace. You can draw flowcharts, org charts, mind maps, UML diagrams, process maps, wireframes, and more using shape libraries and templates, then connect them with smart connectors that stay attached when you move things. An infinite canvas supports brainstorming and planning, and teams can edit together in real time with comments and cursors.

Some features go beyond plain drawing. Diagrams can be linked to data, so a shape can show information from a spreadsheet or tool, and cards and tables let you build lightweight planning boards. AI features generate a diagram from a text description, summarize or expand notes, and suggest ideas for brainstorming. Presentations and exports in common formats help you share work, and integrations connect with Slack, Confluence, Google Workspace, and Microsoft Teams.

item.title: Cronometer
item.description:
Cronometer is for people who want to know what is in their food, not only how much of it they eat. You log meals by searching a database, scanning barcodes, or entering recipes, and the app breaks them down into calories, macronutrients, and dozens of micronutrients. Its data comes from verified sources such as government nutrition databases, which makes it more reliable than apps built mostly on user-submitted entries.

Detailed tracking supports use cases like managing a medical diet, checking for vitamin and mineral gaps, tracking fasting or specific eating plans, and training for sports. Targets can be customized, charts show trends, and the app can connect with fitness trackers and devices to account for activity. Newer features use AI to speed up logging, for example by recognizing foods from photos, though human review is wise.

item.title: Crowdin
item.description:
Crowdin helps teams make products available in many languages. Developers connect their repositories, such as GitHub or GitLab, and Crowdin picks up new source strings, makes them available to translators, and syncs completed translations back, so localization keeps pace with development. It works with files from mobile, web, and game projects, and with content from design tools like Figma and from help centers.

The translation environment supports several workflows. Professional translators, in-house reviewers, and community volunteers can work in an editor with context, screenshots, glossaries, and translation memory that reuses past translations for consistency. Machine translation and AI features pre-translate content and suggest improvements, and quality checks catch errors. Project managers track progress and can order work from translation vendors through the platform.

item.title: CrowdStrike
item.description: CrowdStrike’s core product is Falcon, a cloud-based endpoint security platform. A small agent on laptops, servers, and cloud workloads sends behavior data to CrowdStrike’s cloud, where machine learning and threat intelligence look for malicious activity such as ransomware or hands-on-keyboard attacks. Because analysis happens in the cloud, the agent is light and updates quickly. The company’s detection and response model, known as EDR and XDR, is widely used by large enterprises and governments.

item.title: Datadog
item.description: Datadog is software-as-a-service for watching what your systems are doing. You install an agent on servers, containers, or cloud accounts, or connect it through one of hundreds of integrations, and it begins collecting metrics, logs, and traces. Dashboards and alerts then show how hosts, databases, queues, and services are behaving. The value for most teams is having infrastructure monitoring, application performance monitoring, log management, and real user monitoring in one place instead of stitching together separate tools.

item.title: Deepdub
item.description: Deepdub works with studios, streamers, and media companies that need content in many languages. Its technology translates the dialogue and generates new speech in the target language, in a voice that matches the original performer, with timing that fits the picture. The goal is dubbing that carries over emotion and character, not the flat voice of a basic text-to-speech engine. It supports over a hundred languages and uses licensed voices, which matters for rights and union considerations.

item.title: Derwent Innovation
item.description:
Derwent Innovation serves IP professionals who need thorough patent research. It provides search across patent documents from many countries, with tools to construct complex queries, filter results, and analyze trends. Its distinguishing asset is the Derwent World Patents Index, in which Clarivate’s editors rewrite patent abstracts in clear language and standardize names and classifications, making it easier to find relevant documents despite varying terminology.

Analytics and workflow tools support decisions about filing, licensing, and litigation. Users can visualize technology landscapes, compare competitors’ portfolios, and track legal status, and AI features help with semantic search, summaries, and finding similar patents. Teams collaborate on search results and export reports. Clarivate also offers related products for trademark and scientific research.

item.title: DNAnexus
item.description: DNAnexus gives life science organizations a place to work with very large datasets. Sequencing a genome produces enormous files, and analyzing thousands of them takes substantial computing and careful data management. The platform provides cloud storage, scalable compute, workflow tools, and a catalog of bioinformatics pipelines, so teams can run analyses without managing their own servers. It is built to meet regulatory and privacy requirements for clinical and health data.

item.title: Doxy.me
item.description:
Doxy.me gives clinicians a simple way to see patients by video. A provider gets a personal link; patients click it, enter a virtual waiting room, and join the visit in their browser with no account or app installation. That simplicity matters for patients who are not comfortable with technology, and it suits therapists, physicians, dietitians, speech and physical therapists, and other practitioners.

Beyond video, the paid tiers add features that clinics need. These include a customizable waiting room, patient check-in, screen sharing, group sessions, text message reminders, payments, and integrations with electronic health record systems. Administrators can manage a team of providers under one account, and the platform includes business associate agreements that healthcare organizations need under HIPAA. Newer AI tools offer note-taking from visits.

item.title: Drata
item.description:
Drata addresses the burden of proving security compliance. Companies selling to enterprises are often asked for a SOC 2 report or other certifications, and preparing for an audit traditionally takes months of gathering screenshots and documents. Drata connects to systems such as AWS, Google Workspace, GitHub, Okta, and HR tools, automatically checks whether controls are in place, and collects evidence continuously, so the company remains audit-ready.

The platform covers more than evidence. It manages policies and employee training, tracks vendor risk, supports risk assessments, and offers a trust center that lets customers see a company’s security posture. Auditors can work directly in the platform. AI features help fill out security questionnaires, summarize risks, and map controls across multiple frameworks, saving time for small security teams.

item.title: Dubverse
item.description:
Dubverse helps creators reach audiences who speak other languages. You upload a video or paste a link, and the platform transcribes the speech, translates the script, and generates a dubbed voice track in the target language, timed to match the original. It supports a range of languages, including many Indian ones, and lets you edit the transcript and translation before the voice is produced, which matters for accuracy.

Features support a full localization workflow. You can choose among voices, adjust speed, and edit individual lines, and the platform can add subtitles. An API supports automation for companies that process a lot of content, and a text-to-speech studio produces voiceovers for videos without translation. Typical customers are YouTubers, e-learning teams, news and entertainment publishers, and brands that run content in several markets.

item.title: Dune Analytics
item.description:
Dune made blockchain data accessible. Raw on-chain information is hard to work with, so Dune indexes data from many blockchains into databases that anyone can query with SQL. Users write queries to answer questions such as how many people used a decentralized exchange last week or how much value is locked in a protocol, and publish results as charts on dashboards that others can fork and extend.

The community aspect is a key feature. Analysts share dashboards openly, so you can find ready-made views of NFT markets, stablecoin flows, protocol metrics, and more, and learn from other people’s queries. Dune AI features help generate and explain SQL from natural language, and APIs allow developers to use query results in applications. Data teams use it for research and reporting.

item.title: Embark Veterinary
item.description: Embark’s test starts with a cheek swab at home. You activate the kit, collect a sample from your dog, and mail it to the lab, and results arrive online in a few weeks. The breed report shows a percentage breakdown across hundreds of breeds and how far back each breed appears in the family tree, which owners of mixed-breed dogs often find revealing. It also estimates traits such as coat color and weight.

item.title: Fauna
item.description:
Fauna set out to give developers a database that scaled globally without managing servers. It combined a flexible document model with relational features, offered strong consistency across regions, and was accessed through an API with its own query language, FQL, and earlier through GraphQL. Developers built web and mobile apps on it without running infrastructure.

The company announced that it would wind down its hosted service, and the service closed, with accounts deleted afterward. It also said it would release parts of its technology as open source, so some of the ideas may live on in community projects.

item.title: Finch3D
item.description:
Finch3D addresses the early design stage, when architects test many layout ideas against requirements. You define a building footprint or site, along with rules such as unit mix, room sizes, and circulation, and Finch generates floor plan options that satisfy the constraints and optimizes them for factors like area efficiency. Architects can compare alternatives quickly instead of sketching each by hand.

The tool is built to fit architects’ workflows. It integrates with the design software they already use, including Revit, Rhino, and Grasshopper, so generated layouts can be refined and documented in familiar environments. It supports quick iterations when the brief changes, and provides metrics that help justify choices to clients, such as the number of units or usable area.

item.title: Fitbod
item.description: Fitbod creates workout plans without a human coach. At setup, you give your fitness level, goals, available equipment, and schedule, and it generates a session for each day. The routine adapts as you log sets, reps, and weights: it suggests weights and volume based on past performance, and it tracks which muscle groups have recovered, so you do not train the same area too hard on consecutive days. Videos demonstrate each exercise.

item.title: Fleetio
item.description:
Fleetio helps organizations that rely on vehicles keep them running. It maintains a record for every vehicle, truck, or piece of equipment, including service history, documents, and costs. Preventive maintenance schedules trigger reminders by mileage, hours, or time, which reduces breakdowns and extends vehicle life. Drivers can complete inspections on a phone app, report issues, and log fuel, and shops can manage work orders and parts.

Data from telematics devices flows into the system, so mileage, location, and diagnostic trouble codes update automatically and can trigger work orders. Reports show total cost of ownership, fuel use, downtime, and compliance items, and integrations connect with accounting, fuel card, and telematics providers. AI features help summarize issues, surface patterns, and suggest actions to reduce cost.

item.title: FlowGPT
item.description:
FlowGPT started as a place to share ChatGPT prompts. People post prompts for writing, coding, productivity, roleplay, and other uses, and others can browse by category, upvote the best, and copy them. Over time it added the ability to run prompts directly on the site and to build small chatbot-style apps, so a prompt can become a reusable tool.

The community aspect drives it. Creators gain followers and recognition for popular prompts, and the site hosts character chats and templates for tasks such as resume writing or SEO. It offers a way to learn prompting techniques by examining what others have written. Many of the contributions are playful or experimental, with quality that varies.

item.title: Formant
item.description:
Formant solves operational problems that arise once robots leave the lab. Companies running fleets of mobile robots, drones, or arms need to know what each machine is doing, diagnose problems, and sometimes take control. Formant collects telemetry, video, and sensor data from robots, shows it in dashboards, and raises alerts when something goes wrong, working with robots running ROS or other software.

Teleoperation is a key feature: an operator can view a robot’s cameras and drive or guide it remotely, which helps with situations where autonomy fails. Teams can capture and tag data to improve machine learning models, schedule and analyze missions, and manage software updates across a fleet. Integrations connect with cloud services and business systems, and AI tools help find anomalies.

item.title: Freeletics
item.description:
Freeletics grew out of bodyweight training. The app creates workout plans based on your goals, fitness level, available time, and equipment, with programs that range from short high-intensity sessions to longer strength and running plans. Videos demonstrate exercises, and you log workouts, so the plan can adjust to how you perform and how you feel.

An AI coach is at the center of the experience. It tailors weekly schedules, changes difficulty, and gives feedback, aiming to feel like a personal trainer at a fraction of the cost. The app also provides nutrition recommendations and recipes, mindfulness sessions, and community features. It works with smartwatches and other health apps.

item.title: Geneious
item.description:
Geneious gives molecular biologists a graphical environment for work that would otherwise need command-line tools. Researchers import sequence data from sequencers or databases, then view, align, annotate, and compare it in a visual interface. It supports de novo assembly and mapping of reads to a reference, building phylogenetic trees, designing primers, and planning cloning experiments, so a lab can do many routine tasks in one program.

A plugin system extends it with additional algorithms and workflows, including tools for antibody discovery, metagenomics, and variant analysis. Results are shared through a collaboration feature, and a server product lets teams work with common databases. The software is part of Dotmatics, which also owns other scientific R&D tools. Machine learning appears in specific tools and plugins instead of as a general assistant.

item.title: GitBook
item.description:
GitBook helps teams publish documentation that people can actually navigate. Writers use a clean editor to create pages, organize them into spaces and collections, and publish them as a polished documentation site with search, navigation, and versioning. Software companies use it for product docs, API references, and internal knowledge bases, and the same content can be shared publicly or restricted to teams.

Developer-friendly features set it apart. Content can sync with a GitHub or GitLab repository, so docs can live alongside code and be reviewed through pull requests, and a change request workflow lets teams review edits before publishing. OpenAPI imports generate API reference pages, and integrations connect analytics, support tools, and chat. AI features include an assistant that answers readers’ questions from the docs, AI-enhanced search, and help with writing and editing pages.

item.title: Gretel.ai
item.description: Gretel helps teams get usable data when real data is sensitive or scarce. Developers connect a dataset, such as customer records or medical tables, and Gretel trains a model that produces new records with the same statistical patterns but no direct link to real individuals. Teams use the results to test software, share data across departments, and train machine learning models without waiting for privacy approvals. It also generates text and tabular data for fine-tuning language models.

item.title: Grip
item.description:
Grip focuses on a problem every large event has: people attend hoping to meet the right contacts, then wander the floor without finding them. Grip collects attendees’ goals when they register, such as buying a product, finding partners, or recruiting, and uses matchmaking to recommend whom to meet. People can accept suggestions, message one another, and schedule meetings before and during the event.

Organizers get tools to manage the experience. Exhibitors can see qualified leads and capture them at the booth, sponsors get measurable engagement data, and the event team can track how many meetings happened and how satisfied participants were. A mobile app and integrations with registration systems, CRMs, and event platforms connect the pieces. Typical customers are trade show and conference organizers in industries like technology, healthcare, and manufacturing.

item.title: Headspace
item.description:
Headspace is one of the best-known meditation apps, with a friendly style and a structured approach for beginners. It offers guided meditations of different lengths, sleep content, movement and breathing exercises, focus music, and courses on topics such as stress, anxiety, and relationships. Short daily sessions are designed to build a habit, and progress features encourage consistency.

The company has expanded beyond meditation into broader mental healthcare. Depending on the market and plan, users can access coaching and therapy services, and employers offer Headspace as a benefit. An AI companion, Ebb, provides conversational support for reflecting on feelings and finding relevant exercises. It is meant to support wellbeing, not to diagnose or treat conditions, and Headspace points users in crisis toward professional help.

item.title: Hinge
item.description:
Hinge takes a different approach from swipe-first dating apps. Profiles are built from photos plus written or voice answers to prompts, which give people something specific to respond to. Users like or comment on a particular part of a profile, which starts a conversation with context.

The app uses algorithms to suggest people likely to be compatible, based on preferences and behavior, and has added AI tools such as prompt feedback to help people write better profiles. It limits how many likes a user can send, which encourages more selective choices, and offers premium tiers.

item.title: Homer
item.description:
Homer is built for young children learning to read and explore. After parents enter a child’s age and interests, the app builds a learning path with activities that include phonics, letter sounds, sight words, stories, math, and creative play, and features content from well-known children’s brands. Lessons are short and playful, with characters and rewards that keep young learners engaged.

Personalization is a selling point: the program adapts to the child’s progress and interests, so a child who loves trains or animals gets content around those themes. Parents get progress reports and ideas for offline activities, and the app is designed to be used with limited screen time. Its approach follows early literacy research, and it has been used in homes and in some schools.

item.title: Honeycomb
item.description:
Honeycomb works from the premise that modern systems fail in unpredictable ways. Engineers send rich events and traces with many attributes, and can slice and filter by any of them to find what is different about slow or failing requests. High-cardinality fields such as user IDs are supported, which many tools handle poorly.

Visual tools highlight outliers, compare groups, and follow a request across services, and service level objectives alert teams when users are affected. The platform embraces OpenTelemetry for data collection, so teams can instrument once. AI features let users ask questions in natural language and help interpret data.

item.title: Hopin
item.description:
Hopin offered an all-in-one environment for online events. Organizers sold tickets, ran live sessions on a main stage, hosted breakout rooms and video networking, and set up virtual expo booths, and attendees moved between these areas as if walking around a venue. It grew explosively as conferences moved online, with large funding rounds and acquisitions of other event and streaming companies.

As in-person events returned, demand for virtual events dropped sharply, and Hopin shrank and restructured. It sold its events platform to RingCentral, which continues to operate it as part of its own offering, and the company’s other products, such as streaming and community tools, were separated or spun out. The brand is no longer the same independent business.

item.title: Hopper
item.description:
Hopper started as a flight price prediction app. It analyzes historical and live fare data to forecast whether a ticket will get cheaper or more expensive, and it tells you to buy now or wait. You can watch a route and get notifications when prices drop, and it highlights flexible dates and nearby airports to save money. The same approach extends to hotels and rental cars.

What sets it apart from simple search tools is a set of financial products around travel. Price Freeze lets you lock a fare for a fee while you decide, and cancellation, change, and delay protections give travelers extra flexibility, usually for an additional cost. Hopper also runs a business that provides these travel and fintech features to other companies through partnerships. Predictions rely on machine learning, but they are estimates, and airline pricing can be unpredictable.

item.title: Hudl
item.description:
Hudl made video review standard for coaching. Teams upload game and practice footage, coaches tag plays, and players watch clips on their phones, which replaces the old routine of sitting in a film room with a stack of tapes. The platform supports many sports, including football, basketball, volleyball, and soccer, and it lets coaches create playlists, draw on video, and share feedback with individuals or groups.

The product now includes hardware and AI. Hudl’s Focus cameras automatically follow the action and record games without a camera operator, which makes video affordable for schools and clubs. AI features tag events, cut highlights, and generate statistics, and a recruiting side of Hudl helps athletes share highlights with college coaches. Separate products serve professional teams with advanced analytics and scouting data, such as through its Wyscout and Sportscode lines.

item.title: Insomnia
item.description:
Insomnia is a desktop application that lets developers send requests to APIs and inspect responses. You build requests with headers, authentication, and bodies, organize them into collections, and use environment variables to switch between development and production. It supports REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket, and Server-Sent Events, and can import definitions from OpenAPI specifications.

Beyond manual testing, it supports design and automation. An API design editor helps write specs, test suites run collections of requests with assertions, and command-line tools run tests in CI. Plugins extend functionality, Git sync stores collections with code, and AI features help generate requests, tests, and documentation. Insomnia can store data locally or in the cloud, a choice that matters to teams concerned about privacy.

item.title: Intrinsic
item.description:
Intrinsic works on a long-standing challenge in manufacturing: robots are powerful, but programming them is slow, specialized, and expensive. The company develops a software platform that lets developers build robotic applications, using skills and tools that can be reused across different robots and tasks. The idea is similar to how an operating system and app tools made computers easier to program for a wide range of hardware.

AI and simulation play a central role. Perception tools help robots see and understand objects, motion planning handles collisions, and simulation lets teams test and refine an application virtually before running it on the factory floor. Intrinsic works with robot makers and system integrators, and it has explored combining its platform with advanced AI models so that robots can handle more varied tasks without extensive reprogramming.

item.title: IPlytics
item.description:
IPlytics focuses on the overlap between patents and technical standards. Many technologies, from 5G to Wi-Fi to video codecs, depend on standards, and companies hold patents they declare essential to implementing them. IPlytics links patent databases with standards documents, declarations, and standardization meeting contributions, helping users understand who owns what and how influential each player is.

Typical users are IP and licensing professionals, R&D strategists, and legal teams. They use it to search for standard-essential patents, benchmark portfolios against competitors, find licensing opportunities, and see which companies are shaping emerging standards. The platform includes analytics, dashboards, and data feeds, and AI features help classify patents and find relevant documents.

item.title: Iris Dating
item.description:
Iris Dating tries to reduce the mismatch of attraction. Users swipe on photos, and the system learns their visual preferences, then predicts which other users they would find attractive and shows only those who are likely to find them attractive as well. The aim is fewer, better matches.

The approach uses facial recognition and machine learning on profile photos, which raises privacy questions about how biometric data is processed and stored. Users should read the policy before uploading photos. Dating apps also carry safety concerns, so meet in public places and verify identities.

item.title: Jumio
item.description: Jumio helps businesses confirm that a customer is who they claim to be. A user photographs an ID document, such as a passport or driver’s license, and takes a selfie. Jumio checks the document for authenticity, reads the data, compares the selfie to the photo on the ID, and uses liveness detection to make sure a real person is present, not a photo, video, or deepfake. The process takes seconds and replaces in-person checks.

item.title: Kinedu
item.description:
Kinedu helps parents support their child’s early development. After entering a baby’s age, the app creates a plan with short, playful activities for each day, such as tummy time ideas, sensory games, and language exercises, with videos that show how to do them. Activities are grouped by areas like physical, cognitive, social-emotional, and language development.

The app tracks milestones and shows a baby’s progress against typical ranges, explaining what is normal and when to speak to a pediatrician. Articles and guidance from experts cover sleep, feeding, and parenting questions, and parents can keep a journal of moments. Some features use personalization to adjust suggestions to a child’s progress.

item.title: Landing AI
item.description:
Landing AI is built around data-centric AI, the idea that improving the quality of training data often matters more than tweaking models. Its LandingLens platform lets manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare teams train computer vision models for tasks like detecting defects, counting objects, and classifying images, with a no-code interface that emphasizes labeling quality and error analysis. Domain experts can build models without being machine learning engineers.

The company has expanded into document intelligence. Its agentic document extraction uses vision and language models to read complex documents such as financial statements, forms, and reports, and to turn them into structured data with visual grounding that shows where each value came from. Developers use APIs to add this to workflows.

item.title: Lemonade
item.description:
Lemonade is an insurance company built around software. Customers get a quote and buy a policy in minutes through an app, chatting with an AI assistant called Maya instead of filling out long forms. The company covers renters, homeowners, car, pet, and term life insurance in various markets. Its pitch to younger customers has been a modern experience, low entry prices, and transparent terms.

AI shows up in operations. A claims bot named Jim can approve and pay simple claims quickly, sometimes within seconds, while complex cases go to human adjusters. Machine learning helps assess risk, detect fraud, and personalize pricing. The company is structured so that it takes a flat fee and uses the rest to pay claims, with unused money going to charities chosen by customers under its Giveback program.

item.title: Mabl
item.description: Mabl aims to make automated testing less fragile. Teams record or describe user flows, such as signing in or checking out, and the platform turns them into automated tests that run in the cloud across browsers and devices. A low-code approach means QA engineers and developers can create tests without writing everything in code, though scripting is available when needed. Tests run on a schedule or in CI/CD pipelines when code changes.

item.title: Mapbox
item.description:
Mapbox is the mapping toolkit behind many apps. Developers use its SDKs to embed interactive maps in websites and in iOS and Android apps, with control over styles, layers, and data. Mapbox Studio lets designers customize map appearance, while vector tiles keep maps fast and sharp.
